name: dudo-core
description: Dudo-Core — deployment tooling for the Cloudflare Worker. See wrangler.jsonc.

scripts.//typecheck: Both trees. `packages/testing` was checked by NOTHING until 2026-09-05, which concealed a fixture that had silently stopped composing what production composes while 400+ assertions kept passing — the suites reported on a shape the product no longer had. The gate landed red with 14 diagnostics and was deliberately kept OUT of this script until it was green, because a red gate folded into a green one makes the green one worthless. It is green as of 2026-09-05 and is now part of the gate. Three of the original 14 were exactly the drift it was added to catch.
scripts.typecheck: npm run typecheck:core && npm run typecheck:tests
scripts.//check:contracts: RETIRED 2026-09-05, the same day it was added, and deliberately not by deleting a check. Unsatisfiable request shapes — a `required` field absent from `properties` under `additionalProperties: false` — are now asserted by `packages/testing/suites/contracts/satisfiability.ts`, which is `qa-agent`'s and is strictly richer: same walk, plus a proof that the walker descends into nested `properties`/`items`/`allOf`, plus a mirror control proving it does not flag everything. `architecture.md` §1 assigns the shape — *producer and consumer are both tested against the contract by `qa-agent`* — and this was a test wearing root tooling's clothes. Retired by this repository's own rule for duplicate checks: two checks are both worth keeping only when each would go red on an input the other passes, and this one would not. It found four real defects first, including `login-v1`'s, which is why the suite case exists at all.
scripts.//test: The four suite entry points. Added 2026-09-05 after `qa-agent` pointed out that NOTHING invoked `packages/testing/**` — `typecheck:tests` only TYPE-checks it. So the suites, the six negative controls, the type-negative probe, every registry-coherence check and the contract-satisfiability case were reachable only by an agent typing their paths, and the contract check had just been moved OUT of `typecheck` on the argument that a suite case runs more often than root tooling. That argument was backwards and this script is what makes it true. All four set a non-zero exit code on failure, so it gates correctly. `run-az2-timing.ts` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT and is not an oversight: it is a measurement rather than a test, and its own header records why — a wall-clock threshold on a shared laptop fails for reasons unrelated to the code, and a suite that goes red under load teaches a team to ignore red. The structural proof of equal work lives in `suites/az2-login/equal-work.ts` and holds on any machine.
scripts.//check:source-bytes: Scans every source file for control bytes. WHY IT EXISTS: three NUL bytes in `platform-route-handlers.ts` made `file` report it as `data`, so plain `grep` found NOTHING in a 1,652-line file — no match, no error, not even a zero from `grep -c ''`. It produced a false negative that nearly sent core-agent to build a handler already at line 1202, and it had been silently degrading every search of that file for days, including any security sweep that used plain grep. WORSE, AND THE REASON THIS IS ROOT TOOLING RATHER THAN A LINT PREFERENCE: `git diff` reports such a file as `Bin 11422 -> 13052 bytes, 0 insertions, 0 deletions`. THE REVIEW TOOL IS DISABLED BY THE DEFECT, so everything committed to those files landed unreviewable. On its first run it found ELEVEN bytes in SIX files across FOUR owners — not the three in one that were reported — including `pagination/cursor.ts` and `identity/pre-auth-admission.ts`, which nobody knew about and which sit on the pagination and login paths. Every one is correct in MEANING and wrong in FORM: deliberate domain separators and deliberate test inputs, typed as raw bytes instead of `String.fromCharCode(0)`. It ships with a known-failing input built at run time and refuses to report at all if that self-test does not fire — constructed rather than committed because `Write` cannot emit a NUL and the shell is what workflow.md §9 forbids.
scripts.//check:route-fields: Compares each platform route's declared `fields ∪ objectFields` against its contract's request `properties`, in BOTH directions. WHY: `platform.organizations.create` advertised `display_name` in its contract and did not declare it on the route, and the class refuses undeclared fields BEFORE authentication — so the first client to trust the contract would have failed EVERY onboarding, on the route that creates customers. web-agent found that one by reading, wired the field, and did not send it. This check is what finds the next one, and it found a second on its first run. It reads the three injected confirmation field names from their owning module rather than hardcoding them, so it does not go stale when that mechanism is renamed, and refuses to run if it cannot read them. Population reported against an independently derived expectation rather than as a bare count: 6 of 7 body-carrying routes are comparable, and the seventh states its request in prose because its body is only the injected fields.
scripts.//WHY THESE TWO ARE NOT IN A GATE YET: BOTH EXIT 1 TODAY, ON REAL FINDINGS — five files still carry control bytes, and `platform.organizations.members.resolve` declares `identifier` while its contract publishes `target_identifier`. They are deliberately NOT chained into `test` or `typecheck`, for the reason recorded in `//typecheck` above and applied there first: A RED GATE FOLDED INTO A GREEN ONE MAKES THE GREEN ONE WORTHLESS. The precedent is `typecheck:tests`, which landed red with 14 diagnostics, was held out until it was green, and only then became part of the gate. THE CONDITION FOR FOLDING THESE IN IS THE SAME AND IS NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL: each goes into the gate the day it exits 0, and neither before. Until then they are run by name, and their findings are tracked as defects rather than tolerated as noise — which is the failure mode of a permanently-red check nobody folds in.
scripts.//migrations: LOCAL variants act on the local simulated D1 and are safe to run freely. REMOTE variants act on the deployed database and are a production-class action requiring explicit user approval each time (.claude/rules/security.md §7). They are separate scripts, and named, so neither can be run by accident.
scripts.//deploy: There is no `deploy` script, deliberately. Deployment is gated on C5 and on explicit user approval; a one-word npm script is exactly the wrong affordance for an action that needs a decision.
